Consider the functions $y:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ and $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined by $$ y(x)=[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}-3{x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,f(y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}]. $$ What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]?$
${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))|}_{{x}_{0}}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} $9$
{{field-2}} {{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1} & 1 \\ 1 & 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}2(1) \\ 1-3(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(2{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(2{x}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}-3{x}_{1}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}-3{x}_{1})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 9 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))|}_{{x}_{0}}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} {{field-3}}
$3$ {{field-4}} $9$
$8$ {{field-5}} $24$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $B$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{3}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}=B.
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ by multiplying it by $A$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =BA \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 6 & 9 \\ 8 & 16 & 24\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For $x,y,z\in {R}^{2},$ consider the following functions: 

$$
\begin{aligned} & y(x)=Ax\,\text{where}\,A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & z(y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & f(z)=Cz\,\text{where}\,C=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $z\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $C$ and outputs a vector $f(z)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}=C.
$$

- The function $z$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $z(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ {y}_{2} & {y}_{1}\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=A{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $A$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x))){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}{|}_{{z}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying the Dimensions of a Derivative
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the functions $\mathbf y: \mathbb R^3\to \mathbb R^2$ and $\mathbf f: \mathbb R^2\to \mathbb R^2,$ defined by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/cd2fdbccada4cc5278411db56d86dc72e44aa183fbe9a0c564c4eee587072fef.svg)

Determine the dimensions of the matrix representing the derivative

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) .
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{f}$ with respect to $\mathbf{y}$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

- The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{y}$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix.

Therefore, the product

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf x}= \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}
$$

of a $2\times 2$ matrix with a $2\times 3$ matrix is a $2\times 3$ matrix.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Differentiating the Composition of Vector-Valued Functions
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the functions $\mathbf y: \mathbb R^3\to \mathbb R^2$ and $\mathbf f: \mathbb R^2\to \mathbb R^2,$ defined by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/823c7500670ec7deeb16b8f656904010f2a579d40f8967ee5f9948f93a2d0c3d.svg)
What is 
$\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))$ evaluated at 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/311debaad69f328c5e9acc9ec0b218eded626be5a9e93f5b07837dc4c296fdaa.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{f}$ with respect to $\mathbf{y}$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/46e607310554414649de798f3b01d1965364d6d652e2ab308d4e5c2647d93ca2.svg) we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/950fed4e51766a66f71026c05093c38764bc1f0bc9c4c5136015a4187c2c1154.svg)

- The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{y}$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -{x}_{3} & -{x}_{2} \\ 1 & {x}_{3} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/547759836320b9850df4a70d8ba19a05741412cc0935dcc43caf8224da07fdce.svg) we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/94bf8ffbcce681efde92719b220545ac89cdee324cd4dedf391b62e916a3ee8e.svg)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Differentiating Functions Defined Using Matrices
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the functions $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{y},$ where $\mathbf x\in \mathbb R^3, \mathbf y\in\mathbb R^2,$ and the matrices $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/93f1a584378171c20649f8c1505162f580fad7074bbb73a571b2eff1ef53b57e.svg)
What is $\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_0 = [1, \, 0, \, -2]^T?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{B}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^3.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} = \mathbf{B}.
$$

- The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{A}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} = \mathbf{A}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =BA \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ -2 & -6 & 1 \\ 20 & -10 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Differentiating the Composition of Three Functions
canonical_examples.problem:
For $\mathbf x, \mathbf y, \mathbf z\in\mathbb R^2,$ consider the following functions: 

$$
\begin{aligned} & y(x)=Ax\,\text{where}\,A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & z(y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}-{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & f(z)=Cz\,\text{where}\,C=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

What is $\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)))$ evaluated at ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/7625625edbb65c637775812baec802a512b580b45e94c896764377cd23a0f946.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))) = \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf z} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf z}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{C}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{z}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf z} = \mathbf{C}.
$$

- The function $\mathbf{z}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/aa560155df00efd7959768d56e38ef7fea999b06d2bfe5515b1af01f2184aaf4.svg)
Evaluating at ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/9ee03503efd8d3da6a4aa7e012eef1d0e390d014aa6ceae1b0f18acd82b5c08f.svg) we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/73522ffceb4c0e0f4d3cad330414660ad822609c67a0a0024cdab2cb62c13778.svg)

- The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{A}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} = \mathbf{A}.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x))){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}{|}_{{z}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 7 \\ 3 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Differentiating the Composition of Three Functions

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider the multivariable function $f:\mathbb R^n \to\mathbb R,$ defined by

$$
f(\mathbf y) = f(y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n)
$$

with $n$ independent variables, and $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R^n,$ defined by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/afa5940765a9d39d7f8ab5aeefd4b550434adc0497b1b65845b00e30dd83d1f5.svg)

which is a vector-valued function of a variable $x.$ 

In a previous lesson, we saw that the derivative of $f(\mathbf{y}(x))$ with respect to $x$ is given by the multivariable chain rule.

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_1}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_2}{\partial x} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_n} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_n}{\partial x}
$$

This can be written as a product of matrices as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/1482285b6db08d8b944fd98871736ffebd912d78842ceac6fbad959b9b9e9e6d.svg)

Now, notice that this can be written as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}
= \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}}_{1\times n} \cdot \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}}_{n\times 1}
$$

where

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}$ is the *total derivative* of $f$ with respect to $\mathbf y$, which is a row vector of size $1\times n$, and

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}$ is the *total derivative* of $\mathbf y$ with respect to $x$, which is a column vector of size $n\times 1.$

In the next slides, we will apply this matrix formulation to a concrete example.

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Consider the multivariable function $f:\mathbb R^n \to\mathbb R,$ defined by

$$
f(\mathbf y) = f(y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n)
$$

with $n$ independent variables, and $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R^n,$ defined by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/afa5940765a9d39d7f8ab5aeefd4b550434adc0497b1b65845b00e30dd83d1f5.svg)

which is a vector-valued function of a variable $x.$ 

In a previous lesson, we saw that the derivative of $f(\mathbf{y}(x))$ with respect to $x$ is given by the multivariable chain rule.

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_1}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_2}{\partial x} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_n} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_n}{\partial x}
$$

This can be written as a product of matrices as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/1482285b6db08d8b944fd98871736ffebd912d78842ceac6fbad959b9b9e9e6d.svg)

Now, notice that this can be written as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}
= \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}}_{1\times n} \cdot \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}}_{n\times 1}
$$

where

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}$ is the *total derivative* of $f$ with respect to $\mathbf y$, which is a row vector of size $1\times n$, and

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}$ is the *total derivative* of $\mathbf y$ with respect to $x$, which is a column vector of size $n\times 1.$

In the next slides, we will apply this matrix formulation to a concrete example.

tutorials.name: The Chain Rule for Total Derivatives
tutorials.problem:
Let $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^q$ and $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^q \to \mathbb{R}^m$ be two differentiable vector-valued functions. We want to compute the derivative of the composition $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}))$ with respect to $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

The **chain rule for total derivatives** tells us that

$$
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{m \times n}
=
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}}_{m \times q}
\cdot
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{q \times n}.
$$

Here, the dot denotes matrix multiplication. The inner matrix dimensions match, so this is a valid matrix product.

**Watch Out!** When applying the chain rule for total derivatives, the *order of multiplication matters!* For example, if we swap the order of the matrix products, we'd get an incorrect result:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} = 
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{q \times n}
\cdot
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}}_{m \times q}
\qquad \text{(WRONG!)}
$$

This is incorrect because the inner matrix dimensions do not agree, making it an invalid matrix product.

Let's take a look at a concrete example.

tutorials.content:

tutorials.name: A Concrete Example
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we define
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/11259475d7bcdbbdf2d28e6540f1af92282a188d05dd6d70038b00ec5ab611a5.svg)

Then, we have $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2.$ 

Let's see how to compute the derivative for the composition $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x})).$

The chain rule states that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} 
= \dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}
\cdot
\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{f}$ with respect to $\mathbf{y}$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

- The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{y}$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ is also a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Computing our derivatives, we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/918c4e1af2c1f33f6d056843ee0d038b4b91dc67e8c112c899a05c273d5fcd89.svg)

Then, by the chain rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & 2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1} & -4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This matrix gives us the total derivative of $\mathbf f$ with respect to $\mathbf x.$

tutorials.title: A Concrete Example
tutorials.content:
Suppose we define
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/11259475d7bcdbbdf2d28e6540f1af92282a188d05dd6d70038b00ec5ab611a5.svg)

Then, we have $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2.$ 

Let's see how to compute the derivative for the composition $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x})).$

The chain rule states that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} 
= \dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}
\cdot
\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{f}$ with respect to $\mathbf{y}$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

- The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus, the total derivative of $\mathbf{y}$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ is also a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Computing our derivatives, we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/918c4e1af2c1f33f6d056843ee0d038b4b91dc67e8c112c899a05c273d5fcd89.svg)

Then, by the chain rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & 2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1} & -4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This matrix gives us the total derivative of $\mathbf f$ with respect to $\mathbf x.$

tutorials.name: Verifying the Chain Rule Example
tutorials.problem:
Let's *verify* that our result from the previous slide is correct by computing the derivative directly.

Recall that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/3e421d8e8fdac73c75fbec18f98a7b338ac46083ea0c4d07cd8f07121420dac1.svg)

First, we substitute $\mathbf{y}$ into $\mathbf{f}$ to write $\mathbf{f}$ explicitly in terms of $\mathbf{x}{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/58f11371168007d979c4ffeae1e6643441459b015d7cf7a08e60c5b05e4f93a1.svg) 

Now, we compute the derivative of $\mathbf f$ with respect to $\mathbf x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1} & -4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This agrees with the result we obtained using the chain rule.

tutorials.title: Verifying the Chain Rule Example
tutorials.content:
Let's *verify* that our result from the previous slide is correct by computing the derivative directly.

Recall that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/3e421d8e8fdac73c75fbec18f98a7b338ac46083ea0c4d07cd8f07121420dac1.svg)

First, we substitute $\mathbf{y}$ into $\mathbf{f}$ to write $\mathbf{f}$ explicitly in terms of $\mathbf{x}{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/58f11371168007d979c4ffeae1e6643441459b015d7cf7a08e60c5b05e4f93a1.svg) 

Now, we compute the derivative of $\mathbf f$ with respect to $\mathbf x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1} & -4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This agrees with the result we obtained using the chain rule.

tutorials.name: The Chain Rule for Functions Defined Using Matrices
tutorials.problem:
We can use the chain rule for functions that use matrices in their definition.

For example, consider the functions $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{y},$ where $\mathbf x\in \mathbb R^3, \mathbf y\in\mathbb R^2,$ and the matrices $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/c721b41403d149ac6d97e543aabb22dec2ce200c99e4dccdae09204eb520b555.svg)
What is $\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_0 = [2, \, 0, \, -1]^T?$

Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{B}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} = \mathbf{B}.
$$

- The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{A}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} = \mathbf{A}.
$$

Since these derivatives are constant matrices, the value at $\mathbf{x}_0$ is simply their product. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =BA \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & 14 \\ 2 & -3 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.title: The Chain Rule for Functions Defined Using Matrices
tutorials.content:
We can use the chain rule for functions that use matrices in their definition.

For example, consider the functions $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{y},$ where $\mathbf x\in \mathbb R^3, \mathbf y\in\mathbb R^2,$ and the matrices $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14219585/assets/c721b41403d149ac6d97e543aabb22dec2ce200c99e4dccdae09204eb520b555.svg)
What is $\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_0 = [2, \, 0, \, -1]^T?$

Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{B}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf y} = \mathbf{B}.
$$

- The function $\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ by multiplying it by $\mathbf{A}$ and outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^2.$ Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x} = \mathbf{A}.
$$

Since these derivatives are constant matrices, the value at $\mathbf{x}_0$ is simply their product. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =BA \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & 14 \\ 2 & -3 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Extending the Chain Rule
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we have the following differentiable functions:

$$
\mathbf{y}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^p, \qquad

\mathbf{z}: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^q, \qquad \mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^q \to \mathbb{R}^m
$$

The chain rule can be extended in the natural way as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d \mathbf x} \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf x))) 
= 
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf z}}_{m\times q} 
\cdot 
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf z}{\textrm d \mathbf y}}_{q\times p} 
\cdot 
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm d\mathbf y}{\textrm d \mathbf x}}_{p\times n}
$$

Let's see an example.
